catalog_quote: Whereas a majority of the words in our data are spoken with a falling pitch, there are quite a few examples of words that are spoken with a distinct rising pitch. ... The words in table 9 contrast with falling-pitch words such as ba5a8l ‘hair’, bE5E8R ‘field’, d|5|8z ‘day’, etc. An example of a minimal pair for tone is ma8al5 ‘father’ versus ma5a8l ‘livestock’. Another near-minimal pair is gO8O5R ‘horse’ versus gO5O8r ‘path’. Pending further investigation of the KS tone system, our current conjecture is that KS tone is similar to Shina tone, involving a contrast between two surface tones (high-falling versus low-rising), the occurrence of which is limited to long vowels. Shina has been analyzed as featuring mora accent, with accent within a word falling either on a short vowel, or on the first or second part (mora) of a long vowel. Accent in Shina, and presumably also in KS, is phonetic…

(2) Deciding source: a 22-page first-hand SIL working paper (2005) co-authored by the region's tone specialist; it states contrastive tone with minimal pairs and proposes a Shina-type mora (pitch) accent, with no stress rule — exactly what the record codes ('tonal', qv tonal-OR-pitch accent, the primary-stress rule hedged as the authors hedge). Glottolog 5.1 knows no grammar or phonology of Kundal Shahi; bibliographic searches I could complete (Crossref, archive.org, Glottolog sources.bib, SIL record, Wikipedia bibliography) surfaced only Rehman 2011 (ergativity chapter), Rehman 2011 PhD (language shift), an ELAR deposit, and Baart 2014 (regional survey). None is known to supersede the 2005 tone analysis; Baar
